rationale: The diagonal subset and diagonal embedding are standard; this item also packages the pairing construction and product-basis convention, so it is a semantic reassembly rather than an exact transcription.

The source states that the diagonal map is an embedding and homeomorphism onto its image. The item adds the binary pairing criterion and spells out the inverse projection, without changing the result.
Stacks, Topology Lemma 5.3.1, has exactly the same arbitrary-space hypotheses and both directions. The proof is expanded into the library's closure-and-basis vocabulary.
The UC Riverside notes state the equalizer theorem for two continuous maps into a Hausdorff codomain.
The UC Riverside notes give the same domain, Hausdorff-codomain, continuity, density, and equality conclusion via the closed equalizer.
The Cambridge notes state and prove that a sequence in a Hausdorff topological space has at most one limit, with the same neighbourhood definition.

Hatcher proves compact Hausdorff spaces normal and proves the point-versus-compact separation used for regularity. His normal convention includes Hausdorffness; the item translates this into the library's separate regular/normal and T3/T4 clauses.
Stacks Topology Lemma 5.3.2 has exactly an arbitrary domain, Hausdorff codomain, continuous map, and closed graph conclusion.

MIT Proposition 2.36 and Remark 2.37 state that for an arbitrary topological domain and compact Hausdorff codomain, continuity is equivalent to closedness of the graph. The item's open-box proof is local and makes its finite-choice cost explicit.
McKay's Exercise 1.68 states the equivalent basis-of-precompact-open-sets formulation and its consequence for every open neighbourhood, with Hausdorffness ensuring compact closure.

This is a bespoke synthesis of the diagonal pullback method and the formula-defined-family versus finite-choice distinction. Each mathematical assertion is read directly from the cited on-disk theorem and definitions.
The UCL notes give the same function, f(x)=1/x off 0 with an arbitrary assigned value at 0, as a closed-graph discontinuous counterexample.

The standard theorem in the first source includes the indispensable Hausdorff-codomain hypothesis; the cocountable/indiscrete facts in the second source license the item's explicit failure when that hypothesis is removed.
This is the real-line specialization of the closed-diagonal characterization, with the standard interval-and-triangle-inequality witness written out.

The sources give the cofinite and cocountable definitions, their non-Hausdorff behaviour on infinite or uncountable carriers, and discreteness on countable carriers; the item translates these through the closed-diagonal theorem.
This is the real-line specialization of Stacks Topology Lemma 5.3.2.
The source gives exactly f(x)=1/x for x nonzero with f(0)=0 as a function with closed graph that is not continuous.
This is the standard dense-set uniqueness theorem specialized to the dense rational subspace of the real line and a Hausdorff real codomain.

The particular constant/characteristic-function witness into a two-point indiscrete codomain is a bespoke construction. Continuity, density, agreement on the rationals, and inequality off them follow immediately from the cited on-disk definitions.
The Cambridge notes explicitly state that the cofinite topology on a finite set is discrete and, equivalently through closed singletons, every finite Hausdorff space is discrete.

Hatcher proves the stronger point-versus-compact and compact-versus-compact separation statements in a Hausdorff space. The item specializes the compact set to a finite set and records the finite-choice bookkeeping.
Hatcher defines homotopy, homotopy relative to a subspace, and path homotopy relative to endpoints with the same interval, endpoint, and fixed-subspace conventions.
The notes state that homotopy is reflexive and symmetric as part of its equivalence-relation proof. The item retains a fixed subspace and supplies the explicit time reversal.
The source proves transitivity by the finite closed-set gluing lemma; the item writes the reparametrized two-piece homotopy and preserves a fixed subspace.
The sources state homotopy is an equivalence relation; the item records the same result for the fixed-restriction and fixed-endpoint subcollections.
The source states that composition preserves homotopy. The item separates precomposition and postcomposition and tracks the relative subspace.

Hatcher defines nullhomotopic maps and contractibility by homotopy type of a point, and Exercise 10 gives the equivalent every-map-out formulation adopted here. The nonempty hypothesis makes the equivalence literal.
Hatcher states exactly that a space is contractible precisely when its identity is homotopic to a constant map.
Hatcher gives the same two maps and both composite homotopies as the definition of homotopy equivalence.
Hatcher explicitly states that homotopy equivalence is an equivalence relation. The item supplies the composition calculation omitted there as an easy exercise.
Hatcher explicitly uses the fact that a map homotopic to a homotopy equivalence is a homotopy equivalence, with the same unrestricted spaces and maps.
Hatcher defines a retraction and a deformation retraction with the subspace fixed at all times, exactly matching this library's convention.
Hatcher writes the inclusion and retraction identities and homotopy that make a deformation retract a homotopy equivalence.
Hatcher Chapter 0, Exercise 9, is exactly the assertion that a retract of a contractible space is contractible.
Hatcher Chapter 0, Exercise 12, states exactly that a homotopy equivalence induces a bijection on path components.

The UC Riverside notes use the same straight-line formula for maps into a convex Euclidean subset. This item separately discharges continuity into the subspace codomain and therefore is a detailed semantic expansion.
The source states that any two continuous maps into a convex Euclidean set are homotopic by the straight-line homotopy.
The source states and proves that every convex subset of Euclidean space is contractible by the same formula.
The source states that a contractible space is path-connected and proves it by restricting the contraction to each point times the interval.
The Stony Brook notes give the same sphere, punctured Euclidean space, radial retraction, and straight-line deformation formula.
The Stony Brook notes state the deformation retract; the item records its immediate homotopy-equivalence consequence as a separate corollary.

Hatcher explicitly says not every retraction is a deformation retraction: every space retracts onto a point, whereas deformation retraction to a point forces path-connectedness. The item chooses the two-point discrete specialization.
Hatcher introduces homotopy equivalence as strictly broader than homeomorphism and supplies nonhomeomorphic examples. The item uses the elementary point-versus-real-line specialization.
This is the convex-target straight-line theorem specialized to the full Euclidean codomain.
Intervals and Euclidean spaces are convex, so this is the source's convex-contractibility theorem specialized to those standard sets.
Hatcher's contractibility and homotopy-equivalence discussion licenses the equivalence to a point; the nonhomeomorphism is the item's explicit cardinality specialization.

Hatcher gives exactly the general mechanism: every space retracts to a point, but a deformation retraction to a point forces path-connectedness. The two-point discrete witness is its smallest specialization.
Hatcher's deformation-retraction definition and mapping-cylinder discussion use the same product-interval contraction; this item writes the cylinder formula for an arbitrary space.
The Stony Brook notes give exactly the radial retraction of punctured Euclidean space onto the unit sphere with the same homotopy.
The straight-line homotopy into a convex set is standard in the first source, and Hatcher supplies the fixed-endpoint path-homotopy convention; the item combines them under equal endpoint hypotheses.
